messages.content: I want to design an SSD-backed key-value store that limits write amplification under long-lived snapshots without sacrificing crash consistency. The targets are to reduce total host-written bytes by 30% versus leveled LSM compaction under identical update-heavy workloads, preserve snapshot isolation and acknowledged writes across crashes, and keep p99 reads within 10% of baseline.

That sets a design goal with three constraints to satisfy together. The write target concerns total bytes written by the host to the SSD: under identical update-heavy workloads, the store should write 30% fewer bytes than leveled LSM compaction. At the same time, long-lived snapshots must retain snapshot-isolated views, acknowledged writes must survive crashes, and p99 reads must stay within 10% of baseline. The targets do not, by themselves, specify an implementation or establish that any design has met them.
Why call out long-lived snapshots rather than just write amplification in general?

Because a long-lived snapshot can continue to need an earlier view while updates continue. A design cannot treat an older value as disposable merely because a newer value exists if that older value remains visible to a snapshot. The aim is to limit the writing associated with this situation while preserving the required views; it is not permission to weaken snapshot isolation.
Does the 30% target mean a 30% reduction in SSD-internal writes?

No. The specified measure is total host-written bytes, compared with leveled LSM compaction under identical update-heavy workloads. SSD-internal writes are not named as the metric. A 30% reduction means the host-written total would be at most 70% of that comparison total for the same workload.
What does “identical update-heavy workloads” contribute to the comparison?

It holds the workload condition fixed when comparing host-written bytes. Otherwise, a difference in update activity could be mistaken for a difference attributable to the store design. “Update-heavy” describes the workload category in the target, but no more specific workload mix is given.
Could the design meet the byte target by making reads much slower?

Not if it is also to meet the stated read constraint. Its p99 reads must remain within 10% of baseline. The byte reduction is therefore not a stand-alone objective that can be pursued without regard to tail read performance.
And p99 refers to the tail of read performance, not the average?
Yes. P99 focuses on the 99th-percentile read, rather than an average read. The requirement specifies a 10% allowance relative to baseline; it does not provide an absolute read-latency value.
Is the read baseline defined as precisely as the write comparison?

The write comparison explicitly names leveled LSM compaction and identical update-heavy workloads. The read requirement says “within 10% of baseline” without further defining that baseline here. It would be premature to add a more specific read-comparison setup as though it were stated.
What exactly has to remain true for snapshot isolation?

A snapshot must continue to present the view appropriate to that snapshot, even as updates occur. Limiting write amplification cannot cause a snapshot to see an inconsistent mixture of versions or lose data it is entitled to see. That describes the correctness obligation, not a particular method of retaining versions.
How does the crash requirement constrain the goal?

The design must preserve acknowledged writes across crashes while maintaining snapshot isolation. A reduction in host-written bytes would not satisfy the goal if it depended on acknowledging writes that could then be lost in a crash. The requirement does not prescribe a particular durability mechanism.
Does that say every open snapshot handle must still be open after a restart?

It does not specify that particular handle-lifecycle behavior. It does specify snapshot isolation and preservation of acknowledged writes across crashes. A claim about reopening individual snapshot handles would need an additional requirement.
So this is a target for a design, rather than a report of measured results?

Exactly. The node asks for an SSD-backed key-value store design that limits write amplification under long-lived snapshots, with a 30% host-written-byte reduction against the stated leveled LSM comparison, crash-safe acknowledged writes and snapshot isolation, and p99 reads within 10% of baseline. None of those outcomes is presented as an experiment already completed.
Could we use an fsynced WAL and indexed MVCC runs, parking snapshot-pinned versions in immutable segments while compacting unpinned updates?

Yes—that is a proposed way to address the design goal. The fsynced write-ahead log, or WAL, is the durability component; indexed multiversion concurrency control (MVCC) runs organize versions for reads; and the compaction distinction is between versions still pinned by snapshots and updates that are not. The proposal is to park the snapshot-pinned versions in immutable segments while continuing to compact the unpinned updates. It is a design approach, not yet a demonstrated result against the byte or read targets.
What is the purpose of the WAL in that combination?

Its purpose is to support recovery of writes across crashes. Fsyncing the WAL is the proposed means of making logged data durable. To preserve an acknowledged write, the write must be durable before it is treated as safely acknowledged; the proposal does not spell out a complete acknowledgment and recovery protocol.
Would the WAL alone provide the snapshot behavior?

No. The WAL addresses durability, while the MVCC runs and treatment of snapshot-pinned versions address which version a snapshot can see. Both concerns have to work together, but an fsynced log by itself does not describe how reads obtain a consistent snapshot view.
What does “indexed MVCC runs” imply here?

It means the stored runs contain multiple versions and have indexing to support finding them. MVCC is relevant because a snapshot can require a version other than the newest one. The proposal does not specify an index format, a version layout, or a read algorithm, so it would be too strong to claim a particular p99 read outcome from the word “indexed” alone.
Is a snapshot-pinned version necessarily the latest version?

No. “Snapshot-pinned” means a version is still needed for a snapshot's view. An update may have produced a newer version, while the snapshot still needs an earlier one. The distinction in the proposal is whether a version must remain available to a snapshot, not whether it is newest.
Does “pinned” mean the version stays in memory?

Not here. It describes the version's relationship to a snapshot: the snapshot still needs it. The proposal specifically says to park snapshot-pinned versions in immutable segments, so “pinned” should not be read as a claim that those versions reside in RAM.
Why put those versions in immutable segments?

The proposed separation lets snapshot-pinned versions remain available without treating them as part of every compaction of unpinned updates. An immutable segment is not changed in place. That is the intuition for limiting rewriting under long-lived snapshots, though the proposal does not establish how many host-written bytes it saves.
And compaction continues for the unpinned updates?

Yes. The proposal does not stop compaction altogether: it parks the snapshot-pinned versions while compacting unpinned updates. That distinction is central. It also does not say that every unpinned version can simply be discarded; “unpinned” identifies the side of the proposed compaction split, not a complete deletion rule.
Would immutable segments mean parked versions can never be reclaimed?

No such permanent-retention rule is stated. “Immutable” describes how those segments are treated while they exist; the proposal does not specify when a version ceases to be snapshot-pinned or how segments are eventually reclaimed. Those lifecycle details should not be assumed from this proposal.
How is this meant to help with write amplification?

The idea is to avoid repeatedly moving versions retained for long-lived snapshots as unpinned updates are compacted. Separating the two groups may limit compaction-related host writes. Whether it reduces *total* host-written bytes by 30% versus leveled LSM compaction under identical update-heavy workloads remains a target, not an established consequence of the proposal.
Do writes to the fsynced WAL still count toward that byte target?

Yes. The target is total host-written bytes, so WAL writes cannot be ignored when considering it. Parking versions and compacting updates also involve host writes. The proposal describes a possible way to change the total, not an exemption for any of its components.
Could parking versions make reads exceed the p99 limit?

That remains an important constraint. The indexed MVCC runs are part of the proposed organization for finding versions, including ones needed by snapshots, but the proposal provides no measured p99 reads or guarantee that they remain within 10% of baseline. The write-saving idea has to be considered alongside that read target.
Does fsyncing the WAL settle crash consistency for the whole store?

It supplies a proposed durability foundation, not a complete proof. The store still has to preserve acknowledged writes across crashes and present snapshot-isolated views. The proposal names an fsynced WAL, indexed MVCC runs, and immutable segments for pinned versions, but does not specify all the coordination and recovery details needed to establish those properties.
So the proposal is to separate the work done for snapshot-pinned versions from compaction of unpinned updates, with the WAL and MVCC runs covering different needs?

Yes. Park snapshot-pinned versions in immutable segments, compact unpinned updates, use an fsynced WAL for durability, and use indexed MVCC runs to organize access to versions. That combination is intended to address write amplification under long-lived snapshots without giving up crash consistency or read performance, while the stated targets still require validation.
How can indexed pinned segments keep p99 point-read latency within 10% of leveled LSM as snapshots accumulate?

The indexes would need to make a point read selective: determine which pinned segments could contain the requested key and a version visible to the requested snapshot, rather than searching every parked segment. That is the route by which pinned segments might remain compatible with the latency target. Indexing alone does not guarantee it, particularly if accumulating snapshots leave more segments for each read to consider. The target is a p99 point-read latency no more than 10% above leveled LSM.
Why isn't an index on each segment enough?

An index can make a lookup *within* one segment efficient, but a read could still spend time deciding which segments to inspect. If it has to consult an increasing number of segment indexes as snapshots accumulate, that extra work can affect p99 latency even when each individual consultation is quick. The relevant question is therefore both how efficiently a candidate segment is searched and how many candidates a point read must consider.
Would every read have to check the pinned segments?

Not necessarily. A point read only needs a version appropriate to its requested view. Pinned segments must be available when they hold a version needed for that view, but making them available does not mean every read should search all of them. The indexing needs to help rule out irrelevant segments without ruling out one that contains the required version.
Is it enough to check whether the key occurs in a segment?

Key membership is useful, but MVCC adds a version question. A segment might contain the key yet not contain the version visible to the requested snapshot. Efficient selection would ideally account for both relevance to the key and relevance to the requested view. Whatever selection is used must remain correct for snapshot isolation.
Could a read just take the first matching version it finds?

Only if “first” is defined by a lookup order that actually yields the version visible to that read. Merely finding a matching key in a pinned segment is not enough: a newer or older version may be the one appropriate to the requested view. The performance goal cannot come at the cost of returning the wrong version.
As snapshots accumulate, should I assume the number of pinned segments increases by the same amount?

No one-to-one relationship is specified. The concern is that accumulating snapshots can increase the amount of retained version data or the lookup work associated with it. The question asks whether indexed pinned segments can keep p99 point reads near leveled LSM despite that pressure; it does not give a formula relating snapshot count to segment count.
What would make the tail latency worse even if most point reads are fast?

P99 is sensitive to the slower reads near the tail. For example, if some reads must consider substantially more candidate segments or versions than others, a good typical lookup would not by itself establish a good p99. That is a general risk to examine, not a claim that this proposed design already exhibits it.
Do reads for a current view and reads for an older snapshot raise the same concern?

They can have different lookup needs. An older snapshot may require a version retained in a pinned segment, while another view may not. The 10% target still concerns p99 point reads against leveled LSM; the question does not specify a mix of reads across snapshot ages. A latency claim would need to be clear about which reads its p99 covers.
Could an index avoid touching the data in segments that lack the key?

That is the general purpose of selective indexing: avoid unnecessary segment-data lookups when a segment cannot supply the requested key or version. But consulting the index itself has a cost, and an index must not incorrectly exclude a needed version. Avoiding data accesses helps only to the extent that the overall point-read path, including index work, stays within the p99 limit.
Would it be fair to say the lookup cost must not grow just because snapshots are retained?

That expresses the design pressure, though it is stronger than a proven property here. Retaining snapshots can require retaining versions; the goal for indexed pinned segments is to prevent that retention from turning each point read into a broad search. What ultimately matters is measured p99 point-read latency relative to leveled LSM, not an assertion that lookup cost is completely independent of snapshot accumulation.
How should I interpret “within 10%” in this particular question?

For point-read latency, it means the proposed store's p99 should be at most 1.10 times the leveled LSM p99 used for comparison. It does not mean every individual read must finish within 10% of a corresponding read, and it does not provide an absolute latency in milliseconds.
Does being immutable itself make a pinned segment fast to read?

Immutability means the parked segment is not modified in place. It can make an index over that segment meaningful without accommodating in-place changes, but immutability alone does not establish fast point reads. The read path still has to identify relevant segments, locate the appropriate MVCC version, and keep its tail latency near the leveled LSM comparison.
So what can we actually conclude about the 10% target from the indexing idea?

Only that indexing provides a plausible way to avoid searching all parked versions on each point read. Whether it succeeds as snapshots accumulate is unresolved here. The decisive issue is whether candidate selection and version lookup remain selective enough that p99 point-read latency stays within 10% of leveled LSM while snapshot-visible versions remain accessible.
Here's a hypothesis for the point-read question: an epoch-aware per-key version index keeps p99 point reads at or below 1.10× leveled LSM with 32 long-lived snapshots.

That is a specific, testable hypothesis. The proposed index uses both the key and epoch information to help find a version appropriate to a read, rather than making the read search pinned segments broadly. The predicted outcome is p99 point-read latency no greater than 1.10 times leveled LSM with 32 long-lived snapshots. It remains a hypothesis, not a measured result.
What does “per-key version index” contribute to that idea?

It focuses the lookup on versions of the requested key. A point read asks for one key, so finding that key's relevant versions without examining unrelated keys is the intended advantage. The hypothesis does not prescribe the index's data structure or establish how much lookup work it saves.
And why make the index epoch-aware?

A snapshot read needs the version visible to its view, which may not be the newest version of the key. Epoch awareness is the proposed way for the index to take that view into account when selecting among versions. It must help choose correctly as well as quickly; returning a convenient but snapshot-inappropriate version would not satisfy the design goal.
Does an epoch have to correspond to one of the 32 snapshots?

The hypothesis does not specify how epochs are assigned or how they relate numerically to individual snapshots. It says the per-key version index is epoch-aware and considers the case of 32 long-lived snapshots. Assuming one epoch per snapshot would add an implementation detail that has not been stated.
Is the claim that each point read will be at most 10% slower than leveled LSM?

No. The bound is on p99 point-read latency: the proposed store's 99th-percentile point-read latency is hypothesized to be at most 1.10 times the leveled LSM p99. Individual reads could differ by more or less without, by themselves, settling that percentile comparison.
If it comes out exactly 1.10×, is that inside the hypothesis?
Yes. The hypothesis uses “≤1.10×,” so equality is included. A measured p99 above 1.10 times the leveled LSM comparison would not meet that stated bound.
Why specify 32 long-lived snapshots instead of saying it works as snapshots accumulate?

Thirty-two long-lived snapshots give the hypothesis an explicit condition. The broader question is how lookup latency behaves as snapshots accumulate, but this particular claim predicts the p99 bound with 32. It does not assert the same bound for every snapshot count or indefinitely many snapshots.
Does it predict that adding snapshots has no effect on read latency?

No. It predicts an upper bound relative to leveled LSM under the stated 32-snapshot condition. Some added lookup cost could still fit within that bound. The hypothesis makes no claim that latency is constant as snapshots are added.
How would this relate to the pinned segments we were discussing?

The index is proposed as a way to find a key's snapshot-visible version without treating every pinned segment as an equally likely place to search. Pinned versions must remain accessible for the snapshots that need them. The hypothesis does not specify how index entries refer to segments or how the index itself is maintained.
Could a per-key index still leave a difficult choice among several versions of the same key?

Yes. Narrowing a lookup to one key does not, by itself, identify which of that key's versions belongs to a particular snapshot's view. That is why epoch awareness matters to the hypothesis: the read needs a version-selection path, not just a way to find occurrences of the key.
So is the proposed index guaranteed to avoid checking multiple segments?

No such guarantee is stated. It is intended to make point reads selective, but the hypothesis gives a latency prediction, not a bound on the number of segments checked. Whether any particular lookup checks one or several segments depends on details not supplied here.
Would the index count as successful if it found a fast version but occasionally returned the wrong snapshot value?

No. The design goal still requires snapshot isolation. The latency hypothesis concerns the performance of correct point reads; an index that sometimes returns a version inappropriate to the requested view would not be an acceptable way to achieve a low p99.
Does the hypothesis also establish the 30% reduction in total host-written bytes?

No. It addresses the point-read latency concern. An epoch-aware per-key version index may itself require work to maintain, but the hypothesis does not quantify its write cost or show that the overall store reduces total host-written bytes by 30% versus leveled LSM compaction. That is a separate requirement of the broader design goal.
Nor does a good read result prove acknowledged writes survive a crash, right?

Right. P99 point-read latency and crash durability are distinct properties. Even if the hypothesized read bound held, the store would still need to preserve acknowledged writes across crashes and maintain snapshot isolation. The latency hypothesis does not settle those correctness requirements.
What would a result have to report to speak directly to this hypothesis?

It would need the p99 point-read latency for the indexed design and for leveled LSM under a clearly comparable condition with 32 long-lived snapshots, then compare their ratio with 1.10. The read population represented by p99 would also need to be clear. No such result is supplied here, so the predicted bound remains unverified.
Then the narrow claim is about using key and epoch information to keep the tail of point reads close to leveled LSM at that snapshot count?

Yes. Specifically, the hypothesis is that an epoch-aware per-key version index keeps p99 point-read latency ≤1.10× leveled LSM with 32 long-lived snapshots. It proposes a way to address lookup pressure from retained versions without claiming a particular index implementation or an already observed performance result.
Let's benchmark epoch-indexed segments against leveled LSM under 32 eight-hour snapshots, tracking p99 point-read latency and host-written bytes.

That is a benchmark plan, not a result. It names the two approaches to compare, the condition of 32 eight-hour snapshots, and two measurements: p99 point-read latency and host-written bytes. The latency measurement speaks to whether indexed segments can keep tail point reads close to leveled LSM as snapshots are retained; the byte measurement captures the write cost of the approach.
Does “32 eight-hour snapshots” mean taking one snapshot every eight hours?
No. It describes 32 snapshots with an eight-hour lifetime. It does not specify the interval between creating them or their exact overlap.
Does it say the benchmark itself lasts exactly eight hours?
No. Eight hours describes the snapshots in the planned condition. The benchmark's total duration is not specified by that phrase.
Why track p99 rather than just average point-read latency?

The concern is tail point-read performance. An average could remain low even if a smaller portion of reads became much slower when looking for versions in indexed segments. P99 measures the 99th-percentile point read, making it more directly relevant to that concern.
What comparison would the latency numbers support?

They would allow the p99 point-read latency of the epoch-indexed segments to be compared with the leveled LSM p99 under the benchmark condition. The broader read target is within 10% of baseline, but the plan supplies no numbers yet; it does not say whether the comparison will fall inside that bound.
Do we know whether those point reads are for the latest view or for the snapshots?

The plan does not specify the read population represented by p99. That distinction would matter when interpreting the measurement, because a read requiring an older snapshot-visible version may exercise a different lookup path. We should not assume a particular mix from the benchmark description alone.
Why measure host-written bytes in a read-latency benchmark?

Because the indexed-segment approach is intended to limit writing as well as support point reads. Tracking both measurements keeps the comparison from focusing only on a fast lookup path while overlooking its write cost. The plan does not yet report either measurement or establish a trade-off between them.
Would writes used to maintain an epoch index count?

If maintaining the index causes host writes during the benchmark, those writes belong in the total host-written-byte measurement. The metric is not limited to compaction writes. The plan does not specify how the index is maintained or how many bytes that maintenance will write.
Is host-written bytes the same as writes internal to the SSD?
No. Host-written bytes concerns bytes written by the host to the device. It is not, by itself, a measurement of the SSD's internal writes. The planned benchmark names host-written bytes.
If the two approaches run different amounts of update activity, could we still interpret the byte comparison?

That would make it difficult to attribute a difference in host-written bytes to the approaches themselves. The broader write target compares against leveled LSM under identical update-heavy workloads. The benchmark plan names the approaches and metrics but does not spell out its workload controls.
Does the plan specify the structure of the epoch index?

No. “Epoch-indexed segments” identifies the approach being benchmarked, not a particular index format, placement, or lookup procedure. The plan is about comparing its measured behavior with leveled LSM under the stated snapshot condition.
Could the benchmark tell us exactly how p99 changes for every number of snapshots?

Not from the condition stated here. This plan specifies 32 eight-hour snapshots. A comparison under that condition can speak to that condition, but it does not automatically establish a latency curve for other snapshot counts or lifetimes.
Does tracking those two measurements also test whether acknowledged writes survive crashes?

No. P99 point-read latency and host-written bytes are performance measurements. They do not by themselves demonstrate recovery of acknowledged writes or snapshot isolation across crashes. Those remain requirements of the store, but a crash test is not specified in this benchmark plan.
So the proposed benchmark can address the point-read question without implying that the design already satisfies it?

Yes. Comparing epoch-indexed segments with leveled LSM under 32 eight-hour snapshots, while tracking p99 point-read latency and host-written bytes, is a way to gather evidence about the approach. Until there are measurements, the plan makes no claim that the latency bound or write-reduction target has been met.
Run SnapMix-32 comparing epoch-indexed segments with leveled LSM under 32 eight-hour snapshots, and record p99 reads and host-written bytes.

SnapMix-32 is the named comparison activity: run the epoch-indexed segments and leveled LSM under the condition of 32 eight-hour snapshots, then record p99 read performance and total host-written bytes for each. No measurements are supplied here, so I can describe the run and what to record, but I cannot report its outcome.
What exactly is being compared in SnapMix-32?

The two approaches are epoch-indexed segments and leveled LSM. SnapMix-32 places them under the stated snapshot condition and records a read-tail metric and a write-volume metric. It does not specify further implementation details for either approach.
Does the name SnapMix-32 give us any additional workload details?
No. SnapMix-32 names the activity, and the description specifies 32 eight-hour snapshots. The name alone does not define an update mix, read mix, schedule, or other workload parameters.
What should “record p99 reads” mean in the results?

Record the 99th-percentile read latency for each approach, so their tail read performance can be compared. In the point-read discussion this activity addresses, p99 point-read latency is the relevant interpretation. The activity does not provide a measured p99 or specify the population of reads from which it would be calculated.
And should host-written bytes include only the writes from compaction?

No. Record total host-written bytes for each approach, not just a compaction-only subtotal. Otherwise, the comparison could omit writes associated with the approach being evaluated. The activity does not state any byte totals.
Are the 32 snapshots supposed to be eight hours old when reads happen?

The stated condition is 32 eight-hour snapshots. It does not specify the age of each snapshot at each read, or a schedule for creating and reading them. Those details should not be inferred from the description.
Does saying “run SnapMix-32” mean we already know whether the index meets the read-latency hypothesis?

No. This is the activity that would gather evidence for that question. Recording the p99 values would allow a comparison with leveled LSM, but the instruction to run it is not itself a result or a confirmation of the hypothesis.
Could we claim a write-amplification improvement merely because the activity records host-written bytes?
No. Recording a metric makes the comparison possible; it does not establish which approach writes fewer bytes or by how much. SnapMix-32 names what to measure, not the measured outcome.
Does this activity test crash consistency too?

Not as stated. SnapMix-32 records p99 reads and host-written bytes under the specified snapshots. It does not describe crash injection or recovery checks, so those correctness properties cannot be concluded from this activity alone.
How should the two recorded metrics be presented without overclaiming?

Keep the epoch-indexed-segment and leveled-LSM values identifiable for both p99 reads and host-written bytes, and tie them to the 32 eight-hour-snapshot condition. Until values are actually available, leave the comparison open rather than asserting a latency ratio or byte reduction.
So the immediate action is SnapMix-32 itself, not choosing a winner?

Exactly. Run SnapMix-32 to compare epoch-indexed segments with leveled LSM under 32 eight-hour snapshots, recording p99 reads and host-written bytes. The activity specifies the comparison and measurements; it does not yet supply evidence for a winner.
SnapMix-32 measured 2.14 ms p99 point reads for the epoch-indexed segments versus 2.00 ms for leveled LSM, with 32% fewer host-written bytes.

Those are the recorded SnapMix-32 comparisons under 32 eight-hour snapshots. The epoch-indexed segments' p99 point-read latency was 0.14 ms higher than leveled LSM's: 2.14 ms versus 2.00 ms. They also had 32% fewer host-written bytes than leveled LSM in that comparison.
What is the read-latency difference as a percentage of leveled LSM?
The difference is 0.14 ms. Dividing by the 2.00 ms leveled LSM p99 gives 7%, so the measured p99 for epoch-indexed segments was 1.07× the leveled LSM p99.
Does 1.07× describe each point read?
No. It is the ratio of the two reported p99 point-read latencies. It does not say that each individual read took 7% longer, or describe how the latencies of individual reads were distributed.
Which approach had the lower p99 point-read latency?
Leveled LSM did in SnapMix-32: its reported p99 was 2.00 ms, compared with 2.14 ms for the epoch-indexed segments.
Which approach wrote fewer bytes from the host?

The epoch-indexed segments did. SnapMix-32 reports 32% fewer host-written bytes for them than for leveled LSM. Expressed as a ratio, that is 68% of leveled LSM's host-written-byte total in this comparison.
Can we turn that percentage into a number of bytes?
Not from the reported evidence alone. It gives the relative difference—32% fewer host-written bytes—but no absolute byte total for either approach.
Is the 32% figure an SSD-internal write measurement?
No. It is a host-written-byte comparison. The reported evidence does not give a measure of writes internal to the SSD.
Do the latency figures tell us anything about average reads?
They report p99 point-read latencies, not averages. From 2.14 ms and 2.00 ms at p99, we cannot calculate either approach's mean or median read latency.
Could the difference in p99 be expressed without rounding to a percentage?
Yes. The direct measured difference is 0.14 ms, and the ratio is 2.14 ÷ 2.00 = 1.07. The corresponding percentage difference, relative to leveled LSM's p99, is exactly 7% using the reported figures.
Do we know whether all 32 snapshots were read during the run?

The evidence does not say. SnapMix-32 used the condition of 32 eight-hour snapshots, but the reported figures do not specify which snapshots contributed reads or the mix of point reads represented by p99.
Does the result show how latency changes between one snapshot and 32?
No. The reported comparison is under 32 eight-hour snapshots. It does not provide measurements at other snapshot counts, so it does not establish a trend as the count changes.
Can the host-written-byte result be attributed specifically to moving pinned versions less often?
Not from these measurements alone. They report the total host-written-byte difference between the two approaches, but they do not break it down by cause or by type of write.
And do these figures demonstrate recovery after a crash?

No. The evidence here consists of p99 point-read latency and host-written-byte measurements. It contains no crash or recovery result, so it cannot establish what happened to acknowledged writes across a crash.
What's the narrowest accurate way to state the SnapMix-32 observation?

Under 32 eight-hour snapshots, SnapMix-32 measured p99 point reads of 2.14 ms for epoch-indexed segments versus 2.00 ms for leveled LSM, while the epoch-indexed segments had 32% fewer host-written bytes. That states the observed comparison without extending it to other snapshot conditions or unmeasured correctness properties.
Run SnapMix-Sweep at 1, 8, 32, and 64 eight-hour snapshots, comparing indexed-segment and leveled-LSM p99 point reads.

SnapMix-Sweep is a planned comparison across four snapshot counts: 1, 8, 32, and 64, with eight-hour snapshots at each count. For each condition, compare the indexed-segment approach with leveled LSM on p99 point-read latency. This describes what to run and measure; it supplies no sweep results.
Is this one comparison with four numbers, or a comparison at each snapshot count?

It calls for a comparison at each count. The indexed-segment p99 and the leveled-LSM p99 should be identifiable for the 1-snapshot condition, and likewise for 8, 32, and 64. That lets the comparison be read at each snapshot count rather than collapsing the sweep into a single p99.
What does eight-hour mean when there are 64 snapshots?
It describes the snapshots' duration, including in the 64-snapshot condition. It does not mean the count is 64 hours or specify when the snapshots are created relative to one another.
Why sweep the snapshot count?

The question is how point-read tail latency behaves as snapshots accumulate. Measuring at 1, 8, 32, and 64 eight-hour snapshots can show whether the indexed-segment and leveled-LSM p99 readings, and the difference between them, vary across those stated conditions. The plan does not predict the direction or size of any variation.
Should I compare the indexed-segment reading at 64 snapshots with leveled LSM at 1?

For a like-count comparison, compare the approaches at the same snapshot count: 64 with 64, 32 with 32, and so on. You can also look at how each approach's p99 changes across counts, but those are different comparisons and should be distinguished.
Does SnapMix-Sweep measure average read time too?
Not as stated. The specified metric is p99 point-read latency. The activity does not call for reporting mean or median read time.
Could we use the sweep to report how many host-written bytes each approach uses at 64 snapshots?

Host-written bytes are not a specified measurement for SnapMix-Sweep. Its stated comparison is indexed-segment versus leveled-LSM p99 point reads at the four snapshot counts. It would be inaccurate to present byte figures as results of this activity without a measurement that supplies them.
Is 32 included so we can examine point-read latency at the same snapshot count as the index hypothesis?

Yes. The 32-snapshot condition gives a p99 point-read comparison at that count. The sweep also includes 1, 8, and 64 eight-hour snapshots, which can show how the comparison behaves at other specified counts. No outcome at any of those counts is given yet.
Would a 10% comparison have the same meaning at each count?

As a way of expressing a ratio, yes: an indexed-segment p99 within 10% of leveled LSM would be no more than 1.10 times the leveled-LSM p99 at the same count. The sweep activity itself asks for the p99 comparisons; it does not state that this bound will hold at 1, 8, 32, or 64 snapshots.
Does having four counts tell us what happens at every count between them?

What does separating values from the version index accomplish conceptually?

It allows the design to manage value records and version-finding information as distinct concerns. That separation is intended to offer a way to limit rewriting under long-lived snapshots, but the proposal gives no byte counts or measured savings.

No. An append-only log adds records rather than overwriting existing log records in place. If an earlier value is still needed by a snapshot, the proposal's reclamation rule keeps it from being removed prematurely.

The WAL backing is proposed to support recovery of changes to the version index after a crash. A recovered index must still identify the versions that reads are entitled to see. Is the WAL-backed version index itself the value store?

Not in this proposal. Values are separated into the append-only log. The version index serves to locate or identify the relevant stored version; the WAL backs changes to that index. The proposal does not prescribe the exact contents or representation of an index entry.
What does “reclaim records only after snapshot expiration” protect?

It protects records that a live snapshot may still need for its view. An update can make a newer value available without making every earlier value irrelevant to existing snapshots. The rule prevents reclamation from removing such a record before the snapshot requiring it has expired.
Suppose one snapshot expires while another still needs the same record. Is reclamation allowed?

Not if another unexpired snapshot still needs it. “Only after snapshot expiration” is a restriction on reclaiming snapshot-needed records, not permission to reclaim a record as soon as any one snapshot expires.
Does expiration mean every old record must be reclaimed immediately?

No. The proposal says records are reclaimed only after snapshot expiration; it does not require immediate reclamation, give a schedule, or say that expiration alone makes every record reclaimable. It sets a boundary against reclaiming too early.
Would an expired snapshot still need its old view preserved?

The proposal uses snapshot expiration as the point after which its need to retain records no longer constrains reclamation. An unexpired snapshot's view must remain available. No more detailed snapshot-lifecycle rules are stated here.
Could reclaiming records reduce the total amount written to the SSD?

The proposal is aimed at limiting write amplification, but reclamation itself can involve work and the design's total host-written bytes would include its writes. Whether the append-only log and version index together reduce total host-written bytes by 30% versus leveled LSM compaction under identical update-heavy workloads is not established by the proposal.
Does putting values in a separate log settle the p99 read requirement?

No. A point read must find the appropriate version through the index and obtain its value from the log. Those steps may have latency costs. The proposal does not provide p99 measurements, so it cannot establish that reads remain within 10% of baseline.
Can the index just direct every read to the newest value?

Not for every read. A snapshot can require an earlier version, so the version index must support selecting a version appropriate to the requested view. Sending a snapshot read to the newest value regardless of that view would violate snapshot isolation.
Is the append-only log by itself enough to provide snapshot isolation?

No. Retaining value records makes earlier values potentially available, but snapshot isolation also requires choosing the correct version for each snapshot and avoiding premature reclamation. The log, version index, and expiration constraint have to serve those needs together.
Does this proposal say how large the log or index will become during long-lived snapshots?

No. Retaining records while snapshots need them may affect storage use, but no size, growth rate, or limit is specified. The proposal describes where values go, how versions are indexed at a high level, and when reclamation may occur—not a capacity result.
What would it take to claim this design preserves acknowledged writes across crashes?

The log's values and the WAL-backed version index would need a crash-safe relationship so that an acknowledged write remains recoverable and readable after a crash. This proposal does not specify the full acknowledgment, persistence, or recovery ordering, so that guarantee remains a requirement to demonstrate rather than a proven outcome.
What's the narrowest accurate description of the approach?

Store values in an append-only log, maintain a WAL-backed version index to find the appropriate versions, and do not reclaim records until snapshots needing them have expired. It is a proposed route toward limiting write amplification under long-lived snapshots while still needing to satisfy snapshot isolation, crash durability, and the stated host-written-byte and p99 read targets.
Which value-log and WAL flush order prevents acknowledged writes from referencing missing values after power loss?

If the WAL records a version-index reference to a value stored only in the separate value log, the value must be durable before that reference can be durably committed and the write acknowledged. A candidate ordering is: append the value, flush the value log to durable storage, flush the WAL record that makes the version-index reference recoverable, then acknowledge the write. Otherwise, recovery could restore an index reference whose value was lost. The proposal has not yet specified the complete persistence protocol, so this is the ordering requirement for that reference-based case, not a claim that it has been implemented.
Why isn't flushing the WAL first sufficient? It's a write-ahead log.

“Write-ahead” describes the WAL's role in recovering index changes; it does not automatically make a separately stored value durable. If a durable WAL entry contains only a reference, and power fails before the referenced value reaches durable storage, replaying that entry could produce a reference to a missing value. The contents of the WAL matter as well as its flush timing.
So is the critical rule simply to flush the value log before the WAL?

For a WAL entry that depends on a separately stored value, that is the key durability dependency: make the value durable before making its reference durable. Acknowledgment must come after the persistence needed to recover both. Stating only that one flush precedes the other would be incomplete if an acknowledgment could occur before the required flushes finished.
What happens if power fails after the value-log flush but before the WAL flush?

Under that proposed ordering, the value may be durable while its index reference is not yet recoverably committed. If the write has not been acknowledged, losing it as a visible write would not violate the requirement to preserve *acknowledged* writes. The durable value might then need to be treated as an unreferenced record; the proposal does not specify a recovery or reclamation procedure for that case.
And if power fails after the WAL flush but before the acknowledgment reaches the client?

With the value already durable, recovery should not face a missing value for that durable reference. The client may not know whether the write took effect if it never received the acknowledgment. That uncertainty is different from losing a write that *was* acknowledged. The proposal does not define the client-facing behavior for that interval.
What if the acknowledgment is sent after appending the value but before either flush?

Then a power loss could discard the value and its recoverable index change after the client had been told the write succeeded. That would conflict with preserving acknowledged writes across crashes. Merely appending to an in-memory or not-yet-durable write path cannot, by itself, establish the required durability.
Could we flush the WAL first if it contains the entire value rather than just a reference?

Potentially, yes: if a durable WAL contains enough information to reconstruct the value, the missing-value risk has a different recovery answer. But the proposal only says to use a WAL-backed version index alongside a separate append-only value log; it does not specify that the WAL contains full values. We should not assume that alternative when choosing an order for a WAL entry that merely references the value log.
Does persisting an index entry to its own storage change the dependency?

Another proposal: use epoch-pinned page-map roots and append-only B-tree deltas, consolidating at eight versions with checksum-verified atomic root commits.

That proposes a way to retain snapshot views while limiting how often updates rewrite existing structures. What is the page-map root doing for a snapshot?

Conceptually, it anchors the mapping a snapshot uses to find data. Pinning a root to an epoch means updates must not make that snapshot’s root cease to represent its intended view. The proposal does not specify the page-map layout or how epochs are assigned.

No such rule is stated. The proposed object being pinned is the page-map root for an epoch. Keeping a snapshot’s view available may constrain which referenced information can be discarded, but the proposal does not say that every page is frozen or describe a page-retention mechanism.
Why use append-only B-tree deltas?

The idea is to represent updates as additions rather than repeatedly rewriting an existing B-tree structure in place. That may help limit host writes while older snapshot views remain needed. “Append-only” describes how the proposed deltas are added; it does not establish a measured reduction in total host-written bytes.

It should see the versions appropriate to its snapshot, not simply every later addition. The epoch-pinned root and deltas would have to be interpreted so that later updates do not change the view the snapshot is entitled to see. The proposal does not give the exact visibility rule or lookup procedure.
How does this differ from rewriting a B-tree page on each update?

At the conceptual level, an append-only delta records a change separately instead of modifying an existing page for that change. Consolidation can then combine accumulated versions. The proposal does not specify how many pages any update writes, so that distinction should not be turned into a quantitative write claim.

The proposal specifies a consolidation threshold of eight versions, but it does not define the precise unit whose versions are counted. Not according to this proposal. Eight is a stated design threshold; no experiment or comparison showing that it is optimal is provided.
Does consolidation mean discarding all but the newest version?

No. Snapshot isolation still requires preserving any version a live snapshot needs. Consolidation can be understood as reorganizing versions, but the proposal does not specify its retention or deletion rules. Reaching eight versions cannot by itself authorize discarding snapshot-visible data.
Why consolidate at all if deltas are append-only?

No. The proposal says to consolidate at eight versions; it does not state a maximum number of versions examined by a read, or define how consolidation interacts with pinned snapshot views. A read-cost guarantee would require details that are not given.
What is an atomic root commit meant to protect?

It is meant to make a committed root transition appear as a complete change rather than leave recovery depending on a partly committed root. That matters because the root anchors access to a view. It provides a way to verify the integrity of a root commit when it is read or recovered. A checksum check can help identify a commit record that does not verify; it does not, by itself, make the commit atomic or ensure that everything reachable from the root is durable.

Yes. Atomicity concerns whether recovery sees a complete root commit rather than a partial transition. Checksum verification concerns whether the root-commit information passes an integrity check. The proposal specifies both; neither should be treated as a substitute for the other.
If the new root passes its checksum, can we assume every delta it references survived a power loss?

It poses a trade-off, but the proposal does not establish its outcome. Consolidation at eight versions could limit the delta work needed by some reads, while consolidation itself may write data. With 32 snapshots pinning distinct page-map roots, consolidation also has to preserve the views reachable through those roots. No. Distinct pinned roots mean the snapshots have distinct roots for their views; they do not, by themselves, specify how much data those roots share or how consolidation stores older versions. A claim of 32 copies would add an implementation detail that is not given.
Is the eight-version threshold applied separately to each of the 32 roots?

The proposal says to consolidate at eight versions, but it does not define the unit whose versions are counted. We should not assume the threshold is per root, per key, or per page. The 32 pinned roots and the eight-version threshold are separate stated conditions.

If consolidation materializes a combined representation, producing that representation involves writes from the host. Whether those writes are outweighed by writes avoided elsewhere is the question. It could contribute to a lower total if its resulting organization avoids enough subsequent writing, but that cannot be concluded from the threshold. Not necessarily. They constrain what consolidation can make inaccessible: a live snapshot must still be able to use its pinned root to obtain its appropriate view. Could we reclaim an old version as soon as eight versions have accumulated?

Not simply because the threshold was reached. Eight versions is the proposed consolidation trigger, not a rule permitting deletion of versions needed by the 32 snapshots. Reclamation would have to respect each snapshot's view.

Accumulated deltas can leave a point read with version information to examine. Consolidation could reduce that work for some reads by reorganizing those versions. But a read might also need information retained for an older pinned root, so the threshold alone does not tell us its lookup path or latency.

What about using WAL-durable, copy-on-write hash buckets with snapshot-pinned bucket generations and bounded version-chain indexes to avoid rewriting cold values?

That is another proposed organization for the SSD-backed key-value store. Updates would use copy-on-write hash buckets, while snapshots retain access to the bucket generations needed for their views. What does copy-on-write mean for a hash bucket here?

Conceptually, an update creates a new bucket representation rather than modifying a bucket representation in place. That leaves an earlier generation available when a snapshot still needs it. Does snapshot-pinned mean an old generation can never be removed?
No. It means a generation needed by a live snapshot must remain available to that snapshot. The proposal does not specify when generations cease to be pinned or how they are eventually reclaimed.
Why pin generations rather than just keep the newest bucket?

A snapshot may need to see a view from before a later update. If only the newest bucket generation remained accessible, that snapshot could lose the versions appropriate to its view. Pinning the needed generation is the proposal’s way of keeping that earlier view reachable.
Is a bucket generation the same thing as a value version?

Not necessarily. A bucket generation describes a representation of a bucket at a particular stage, while a value version concerns the value visible for a key. The proposal uses both bucket generations and version-chain indexes, but does not define a one-to-one relationship between them.
What is the WAL meant to make durable?

The WAL is the proposed durability mechanism for recoverable updates to this bucket-based design. For acknowledged writes to survive a crash, recovery would need to reconstruct the appropriate bucket and version state. Calling the design WAL-durable expresses that intent; it does not provide a complete write, acknowledgment, or recovery sequence.
Could we acknowledge a write as soon as its new bucket has been built?

Not merely because a new representation has been built. Does copy-on-write itself guarantee crash consistency?

No. Keeping an earlier representation unchanged can be useful for recovery, but a crash-safe transition also has to ensure that recovery uses a complete, durable state and does not lose an acknowledged update. The proposal names a WAL-durable approach without specifying or proving the complete transition protocol.
What are bounded version-chain indexes supposed to do for reads?

They are intended to help a read locate the version appropriate to its view without following an indefinitely growing chain as updates and snapshots accumulate. “Bounded” signals a limit on that lookup structure, but the proposal gives no numerical bound or indexing method. It therefore does not establish a particular p99 latency.
Does bounded mean every read checks at most eight versions?

No. There is no eight-version limit in this proposal. It says only that the version-chain indexes are bounded; it does not state the bound’s value or translate it into a maximum number of versions examined by an individual read.
Would the index be allowed to skip an old version that a pinned snapshot needs?

No. Bounding lookup work cannot come at the expense of snapshot isolation. A read for a pinned snapshot must still be able to find the version appropriate to that snapshot, even when newer bucket generations exist.
Does a hash bucket automatically make point reads fast?

It gives the proposal a way to organize lookups by key, but point-read latency also depends on finding the right bucket generation and version. Snapshot pinning and version lookup can add work. The proposal provides no measured p99 reads, so fast point reads cannot be assumed from the use of hashing alone.
How do the bounded indexes and pinned generations fit together?

Pinned generations keep snapshot-needed bucket states available; version-chain indexes are intended to help select the relevant version within the available states. Both matter: retaining a version is insufficient if a read cannot find it, and finding a pointer quickly is insufficient if the required generation has been discarded. The proposal does not specify their precise relationship in the lookup path.
Why call out cold values?

The stated aim is to avoid rewriting values that are not themselves being updated simply because other updates are occurring. Keeping snapshot-needed bucket generations and using copy-on-write changes is proposed as a way to separate updating from repeatedly moving such cold values. The proposal does not quantify how often cold values would otherwise be rewritten.
Does that mean copy-on-write never rewrites a cold value?

That is stronger than the proposal states. Avoiding cold-value rewrites is its objective, but copy-on-write can itself write new representations. Without a specified bucket layout or measured write breakdown, we cannot claim that no cold value is ever copied.
Would retaining older bucket generations increase storage use?

It can require space while snapshots need those generations. The proposal does not provide a storage-usage bound or a reclamation policy. The relevant obligation is to retain snapshot-visible information; the amount of space needed to do that remains unspecified.
How would we assess whether this helps the write target?

The broader target is 30% fewer total host-written bytes than leveled LSM compaction under identical update-heavy workloads. Could we compare only the bucket writes against leveled LSM compaction writes?

What does this proposal say about the p99 read limit?

If a read is for an older snapshot, can it simply use the newest bucket generation?

Not unless that path returns the version visible to the older snapshot. The point of snapshot-pinned generations is to keep earlier views accessible despite later updates. The proposal does not state that a newest-generation lookup alone suffices for every snapshot read.
Does pinning generations mean updates stop while a snapshot stays open?

No. Copy-on-write is proposed precisely as a way to create changed bucket representations while retaining generations needed by snapshots. The proposal does not say that long-lived snapshots block updates.
Is the proposal a tested design or a set of design elements?

It is a set of proposed design elements: WAL durability, copy-on-write hash buckets, snapshot-pinned bucket generations, and bounded version-chain indexes, with the aim of avoiding cold-value rewrites. It states no benchmark result or completed crash-recovery test for this approach.
What's the main correctness risk to keep distinct from write volume?

Snapshot reads must retain access to their appropriate versions, and acknowledged updates must remain recoverable across crashes. Why does bucket size affect rewrite bytes in a copy-on-write design?

Is the bounded version-chain index supposed to remove the read-side trade-off?
